passage: Thursday night. Project marks are out. Simran got 9 out of 10 for a design almost the same as mine, and I got 6. Same materials, same report length, and mine had the extra test. The professor wrote "excellent teamwork" on hers, and Simran drinks tea in the professor's cabin every Friday. I was so angry I could not eat. Then I made myself list facts: the rubric, both marks, the date I submitted. I am not going to say anything against Simran, because the marking was not her doing. Tomorrow I will email the course coordinator and ask for a recheck against the rubric. And I am still finishing my next report properly, because sulking would only cost me. 😔 Maria

qa.q: How many marks did Simran get?
How did Maria feel about the marks, and why did Maria decide not to say anything against Simran?
qa.a: Maria was so angry about the marks that eating was impossible, but saw that the marking was not Simran's doing, so the complaint is aimed at the rubric and the process.

qa.q: What did Maria plan to do, and why might it work?
qa.a: She plans to email the course coordinator for a recheck against the rubric, which rests on facts like the marks and submission date rather than on anger. 🙂

qa.q: How might Simran feel if Maria's complaint reached her?
qa.a: Simran might feel embarrassed or worried about being blamed, which is why Maria keeps the focus on the process.

grounding: A student sees grades going to a favourite and gathers facts, plans a formal request and keeps her own standards.

passage:
Salma, you asked why I've been so quiet in the design studio. Okay. Our guide keeps giving the client projects to Parth. Four out of four this year, even when my portfolio scored higher in the internal review.
First I got bitter. My next two submissions were lazy, because what was the point? My marks dropped, and that made me even angrier.
Then my senior said, "Bitterness is only hurting you. Get the facts." So I made a sheet: every project, who got it, the review scores. I wasn't imagining it.
I asked for a meeting with the course coordinator, not the guide, and took the sheet. I stayed calm. I said I wanted to understand how projects were allocated. She said she'd look into it and asked for next term's allocations to be shared openly.
Nothing's changed yet. But my own work is back to my standard, because that part I control. So that's me, Rashmi, fighting it properly.

qa.q: How many of this year's client projects went to Parth?
How did Rashmi feel before gathering the facts?
qa.a: Bitter and angry, turning in lazy work because it felt pointless.

qa.q: How did Rashmi raise the unfairness properly?
qa.a: She made a sheet of projects, allocations and scores, met the course coordinator calmly, and asked how projects were allocated.

qa.q: How might the course coordinator see Rashmi's approach?
qa.a: As calm and backed by evidence, which made it easy to take seriously and to ask for open allocations.

grounding: Shows favouritism in project allocation, the harm of bitterness, and gathering facts and using proper channels while keeping one's standards.

passage:
Monday: The lab's only summer research slot went to Dhruv, Professor Rao's nephew, although Shreya had the highest lab grade in the batch. In the corridor Zeenat said, "That's rigged." Shreya went home and didn't open her books.
Wednesday: She almost skipped the next lab report. Then she thought: letting her work slide would prove nothing except that the slot hadn't mattered to her. She wrote the report properly and, that night, listed the facts: the grades, the call for applications, and the date the slot was announced, three days before the deadline.
Friday: With Zeenat beside her for support, she took the list to the head of department's weekly open hour and asked calmly how the slot had been decided, and whether it could be advertised openly next year. The head took notes and promised to review the process. Shreya's report came back that afternoon: 19 out of 20.

qa.q: Who got the lab's summer research slot?
What was Shreya feeling on Monday night?
qa.a: Hurt and discouraged, so much that she didn't open her books.

qa.q: What did Shreya do instead of letting bitterness damage her work?
qa.a: She wrote the report properly, listed the facts, and raised the question calmly at the head of department's open hour.

qa.q: How did Zeenat see the allocation?
qa.a: As rigged, and she supported Shreya by going with her to the open hour.

grounding: Illustrates a research slot going to a favourite, and gathering facts, raising it through proper channels and keeping one's own standards.
